title: Spinal Cord Injury
subject: Surgery
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a life‑threatening event where the cord is damaged by trauma or disease, leading to motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction. Rapid assessment, stabilization and early management are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: SCI is defined by loss of function of the spinal cord due to mechanical injury or secondary pathology. Diagnosis relies on history, clinical exam and imaging when available.
b: History of sudden onset paralysis or loss of sensation
Neurological level and ASIA impairment scale
Plain X‑ray for bony injury
CT preferred over MRI if urgent

t.b: Shows vertebral fracture or dislocation – confirms bony injury; normal X‑ray does not exclude SCI
Detects fracture, canal compromise and early hemorrhage – best first imaging when available
Reveals cord edema, hemorrhage, disc herniation and spinal cord compression – used when time and resources allow

sections.p: SCI is staged by the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS).
b: AIS A – complete loss of motor and sensory function below injury level
AIS B – sensory only
AIS C – some motor function, <50% of key muscles grade 3 or more
AIS D – useful motor function, >50% of key muscles grade 3 or more
AIS E – normal function

t.b: Determines motor and sensory scores; guides prognosis and rehabilitation

sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa, trauma dominates, followed by infectious and metabolic causes.
b: Road traffic crashes – most common in young adults
Falls from height – especially in mining or construction
Gunshot or stab wounds – rural conflict areas
Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease) – endemic in TB‑high regions
HIV‑associated myelopathy
Sickle cell crisis causing cord infarction
Herbal or traditional remedies causing neurotoxicity

t.b: Presents with back pain, fever, weight loss; imaging shows vertebral destruction and epidural abscess – treat with anti‑TB drugs and decompression if needed

sections.p: Presentation depends on level and completeness. Common features include sudden paralysis, loss of sensation, bladder dysfunction and autonomic instability.
b: Motor loss – flaccid initially, then spastic after 24–48 hrs
Sensory loss – dermatomal pattern below injury
Bladder retention or incontinence
Neurogenic shock – hypotension, bradycardia

t.b: Causes hypotension with relative bradycardia; treat with fluid resuscitation and vasopressors

sections.p: Prioritize imaging and basic labs; use bedside tests when resources are limited.

t.b: Checks for anemia or infection that may worsen SCI
Hyponatremia or hypokalemia can worsen neurological status
Detects urinary tract infection, common in SCI patients

sections.p: Early recognition of complications prevents mortality.
b: Spinal shock – transient loss of reflexes
Neurogenic shock – hypotension
Infection – meningitis, epidural abscess
Pressure sores
Deep vein thrombosis
Urinary retention

sections.p: Immediate goals: stabilize, prevent secondary injury, and treat underlying cause.
b: Immobilise spine with rigid board or cervical collar
Maintain spinal cord perfusion – keep MAP >85 mmHg with fluids and vasopressors
Early surgical decompression if CT shows canal compromise (within 24 hrs)
Treat infections aggressively
Manage neurogenic shock
Initiate early mobilisation and physiotherapy

t.b: Crystalloids to maintain MAP; avoid hypotonic solutions
Used when MAP <85 mmHg despite fluids
Broad‑spectrum for suspected infection; adjust per culture

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on rehabilitation and prevention of secondary complications.
b: Regular neuro‑exams
Bladder management
Skin inspection for pressure sores
Vaccination against TB and influenza
Education on safe driving and fall prevention

t.b: Tracks recovery of motor and sensory function

sections.p: Conditions that mimic SCI but have different management.
b: Peripheral neuropathy – sensory loss but preserved reflexes
Spinal epidural abscess – similar pain but progressive fever and systemic signs
Spinal cord infarction – sudden onset but often vascular risk factors

t.b: Loss of reflexes and sensory loss are absent

sections.p: Certain tests may give false negatives in low‑resource settings.
b: Plain X‑ray may miss subtle fractures
CT may not detect early cord edema
MRI often unavailable – rely on clinical exam

t.b: May miss cord contusion; clinical exam remains gold standard

whenToSeekHelp: Severe back pain with neurological deficit
New or worsening weakness after trauma

faq.q: What is the first step after a suspected SCI?
faq.a: Immobilise the spine and maintain spinal cord perfusion while arranging urgent imaging.
Higher MAP improves blood flow to the injured cord and reduces secondary ischemia.

faq.q: Can a patient with incomplete SCI recover fully?
faq.a: Yes, especially if early decompression and rehabilitation are initiated; prognosis depends on injury level and completeness.

exam: What is the most important initial management step after a suspected SCI? — Immobilise spine, maintain MAP >85 mmHg, and arrange urgent imaging.
How would you differentiate neurogenic shock from septic shock in a patient with SCI? — Neurogenic shock shows hypotension with bradycardia and no fever; septic shock has fever and tachycardia.
What imaging modality is preferred if MRI is unavailable? — CT scan, as it rapidly detects fractures and canal compromise.
Why is early surgical decompression within 24 hrs recommended? — It reduces secondary injury and improves neurological recovery.
What is the main cause of pressure sores in SCI patients? — Immobility and loss of sensation leading to prolonged pressure.
What drug class is avoided in SCI patients with neurogenic shock? — Anticholinergic drugs, as they worsen hypotension.
